results.name: above_vs_below_span_asymmetry
results.description: Yes-rate for targets larger than every example minus yes-rate for targets smaller than every example (multi-example sets); the model's span term is symmetric, so observed > null means people extend upward more readily than downward (observed < null: downward more readily).
results.code:
# name: above_vs_below_span_asymmetry
# description: Yes-rate for targets larger than every example minus yes-rate for targets smaller than every example (multi-example sets); the model's span term is symmetric, so observed > null means people extend upward more readily than downward (observed < null: downward more readily).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",")
    n = ex.str.len().values
    lo = ex.map(lambda l: min(int(x) for x in l)).values
    hi = ex.map(lambda l: max(int(x) for x in l)).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    a = (t > hi) & (n >= 2)
    b = (t < lo) & (n >= 2)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: set_size_parity_consistent_gap
results.description: Among parity-homogeneous sets, yes-rate for parity-consistent targets in 3-4-example sets minus in 1-2-example sets; observed < null means people narrow generalization with more examples (a size-principle effect the model lacks), observed > null means more examples make people more permissive than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: set_size_parity_consistent_gap
# description: Among parity-homogeneous sets, yes-rate for parity-consistent targets in 3-4-example sets minus in 1-2-example sets; observed < null means people narrow generalization with more examples (a size-principle effect the model lacks), observed > null means more examples make people more permissive than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",")
    n = ex.str.len().values
    par = ex.map(lambda l: (lambda p: p[0] if len(set(p)) == 1 else -1)([int(x) % 2 for x in l])).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    cons = (par >= 0) & ((t % 2) == par)
    a = cons & (n >= 3)
    b = cons & (n <= 2)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: any_example_digit_overlap_effect
results.description: In multi-example sets, yes-rate for targets sharing at least one digit with at least one example (surface similarity) minus targets sharing no digit with any example; the model only uses digits common to all examples, so observed > null means people use partial surface digit similarity the model ignores (observed < null: the reverse).
results.code:
# name: any_example_digit_overlap_effect
# description: In multi-example sets, yes-rate for targets sharing at least one digit with at least one example (surface similarity) minus targets sharing no digit with any example; the model only uses digits common to all examples, so observed > null means people use partial surface digit similarity the model ignores (observed < null: the reverse).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    n = (s.str.count(",") + 1).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).astype(str)
    digs = s.str.replace(",", "", regex=False)
    share = np.zeros(len(df), bool)
    for d in "0123456789":
        share |= (t.str.contains(d, regex=False).values & digs.str.contains(d, regex=False).values)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    a = (n >= 2) & share
    b = (n >= 2) & ~share
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: sharp_rejection_item_fraction
results.description: Fraction of distinct (set, target) items whose mean yes-rate is <= 1/9 (near-unanimous rejection); observed > null means the model's graded overlap is too soft and under-produces the all-or-none rule-based rejections people make (observed < null: it over-produces them).

results.name: outside_span_proximity_gradient
results.description: Among targets outside the examples' [min,max] range (multi-example sets), yes-rate for targets within 10 of the range minus those more than 10 away; the model treats all out-of-span targets alike, so observed > null means people show a graded numeric-proximity generalization the model lacks (observed < null: the reverse).
results.code:
# name: outside_span_proximity_gradient
# description: Among targets outside the examples' [min,max] range (multi-example sets), yes-rate for targets within 10 of the range minus those more than 10 away; the model treats all out-of-span targets alike, so observed > null means people show a graded numeric-proximity generalization the model lacks (observed < null: the reverse).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",")
    n = ex.str.len().values
    lo = ex.map(lambda l: min(int(x) for x in l)).values
    hi = ex.map(lambda l: max(int(x) for x in l)).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    dist = np.where(t < lo, lo - t, np.where(t > hi, t - hi, 0))
    out = (dist > 0) & (n >= 2)
    near = out & (dist <= 10)
    far = out & (dist > 10)
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[far].mean())

results.name: set_gcd_divisibility_effect
results.description: In multi-example sets whose examples' greatest common divisor g is >= 3, yes-rate for targets divisible by g minus targets not divisible by g; observed > null means people generalize along the examples' exact common divisor (e.g. 15/45 for 90,45; 28 for 84,56; 13 for 13,91), which the model's fixed multiple-of-3..12 list misses (observed < null: the reverse).
results.code:
# name: set_gcd_divisibility_effect
# description: In multi-example sets whose examples' greatest common divisor g is >= 3, yes-rate for targets divisible by g minus targets not divisible by g; observed > null means people generalize along the examples' exact common divisor (e.g. 15/45 for 90,45; 28 for 84,56; 13 for 13,91), which the model's fixed multiple-of-3..12 list misses (observed < null: the reverse).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",")
    n = ex.str.len().values
    g = ex.map(lambda l: math.gcd(*[int(x) for x in l]) if len(l) > 1 else int(l[0])).values.astype(int)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    ok = (n >= 2) & (g >= 3)
    div = (t % np.maximum(g, 1)) == 0
    a = ok & div
    b = ok & ~div
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: odd_x3_parity_vs_multiple_tradeoff
results.description: In sets (>=2 examples) whose examples are all odd and all multiples of 3, yes-rate for odd non-multiples of 3 minus even multiples of 3; observed > null means the model under-weights parity relative to the shared multiple-of-3 rule in these sets (observed < null: over-weights parity).
results.code:
# name: odd_x3_parity_vs_multiple_tradeoff
# description: In sets (>=2 examples) whose examples are all odd and all multiples of 3, yes-rate for odd non-multiples of 3 minus even multiples of 3; observed > null means the model under-weights parity relative to the shared multiple-of-3 rule in these sets (observed < null: over-weights parity).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ex = s.str.split(",")
    n = ex.str.len().values
    ok = ex.map(lambda l: all(int(x) % 2 == 1 and int(x) % 3 == 0 for x in l)).values & (n >= 2)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    a = ok & (t % 2 == 1) & (t % 3 != 0)
    b = ok & (t % 2 == 0) & (t % 3 == 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: trial_position_drift
results.description: Yes-rate on trials in the later half of the session (trial_index above median) minus the earlier half; the model has no trial-order term, so observed far from null means people's yes-bias drifts over the session (observed > null: more yes later; < null: fewer yes later).
